en: The Ritual Manual for Protecting Life and Releasing Creatures, composed by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing of the Tang Dynasty.
Now, as for those who cherish life, they all love their own lives; this sentiment extends upward through the wise and virtuous, and even among those who have died, it is universally present.
Fearing death,
[this extends] down to even the smallest insects;
for this reason, the Sugata cultivates loving-kindness according to each circumstance.
He does not harm sentient beings;
he measures his own body as a standard for others,
and rather than employing blades or staves, he relies solely on great compassion.
He propagated the transformative teachings of the Dharma and applied himself with the utmost earnestness in places dedicated to protecting living beings.
As a disciple of the Buddha,
one ought to act accordingly:
observe for insects and filter the water.
This is the essential protocol for those who have left the household life.
To perceive peril and provide protection is the most urgent form of succor within compassion.
Once it is known that there are insects,
the Vinaya texts prescribe the making of a device for releasing them;
this is solely because such a practice has long been established in the Western Regions (India).
Since everyone understands that this was previously unknown in the Eastern Lands,
it is also necessary to explain its ritual procedures in detail;
if they were not fully set forth, [the matter would remain obscure].
There is no means by which they may attain awakening.
Their vessels for use are made of iron, copper, clay, or wood;
those of clay are provided with handles, while those of iron and wood are fashioned accordingly.
If you intend to carry it with you,
it may be made of copper;
it should hold only two or three *sheng*.
This is simply an old small copper vessel;
restore the copper fastening so that the hand may pass through it.
On one side of the base,
a copper knob must be installed,
capable of holding a small plum blossom or a finger.
When going out to beg for alms,
it should be worn on the left arm and covered with a robe.
Carrying his alms bowl in his right hand,
he went begging for food; having obtained some,
he proceeded to a certain house.
Having set down the alms bowl,
he himself took a single strand of pure rope,
as thick as a coarse chopstick.
According to the depth of the well,
one ties a jar to draw water and filters it through a small strainer.
Having adjusted it until it was sufficient,
he then threaded one end of a cord through the button and tied it tightly with a hitch-knot and other such bindings.
Attach a small iron hook;
when pulling it up,
ensure that it remains level and stable.
These must all be prepared in advance;
one may not seek them out at the last moment.
Thus, using a small strainer.
Cover the jar with insects and lower it slowly;
when it reaches the water, release the hook.
He pulled the rope to cover [the opening],
washed it down two or three times,
and only then drew him out of the well.
This is the protocol for begging for alms.
One may use either a copper bowl or a lacquered bowl;
holes are pierced [in the rim] and cords are attached.
It may also be used as a temporary measure.
If one is in a monastery,
one should cover it with an ordinary iron vessel.
It is to be installed as previously described,
with this slight variation:
iron rings are attached to its base and sides.
It should accommodate three fingers.
Insert the jar-hook (kumbhaka-haṅku) inside it,
lift it up, and fasten it as before by means of the hook.
Place the insects inside a container and release them into water;
even in the case of a deep well, one may proceed in this manner.
If one were to keep a separate rope,
it would likely cause unnecessary trouble;
furthermore, if the well is deep...
Alternatively, one may store it separately in a basin,
or transport it to a river or pond;
once the water has been poured out, [one should proceed].
One must still wash the vessel;
such is the method.
This is the design of the water-strainer.
As stated elsewhere,
how could one possibly spread a strainer over the mouth of a well when there is fundamentally no vessel for releasing living beings?
One’s desire is like guarding the precepts;
one would rather risk the death of insects than do otherwise,
solely for the sake of the Tathāgata’s holy teaching.
Compassion is the foundation.
Among the precepts established, there are both natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and prohibited offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*).
Regarding prohibitions, they accord with the facts and conform to the sūtras;
as for their nature, it logically follows that the more serious should take precedence.
Within the category of natural offenses (prakṛti-sāvadya):
Killing is the foremost [of the unwholesome actions];
therefore, the wise should especially preserve and protect it.
If one treats this as something trivial, [one will suffer the consequences].
What could be more weighty than this?
If one can act in accordance with the teachings,
one will obtain the karmic fruit of long life in the present life.
In a future life, you shall be reborn in the Pure Land.
Furthermore, within the land of China,
there are more than four hundred cities.
Among those who have left the household life, there are tens of thousands by the count;
yet, few are those who apply their minds to the matter of filtering water.
Due to long-standing customs and habitual ways,
Buddhism is held in low regard;
it is impossible to reach everyone door-to-door or transmit the teachings orally.
I hope that all practitioners will instruct and train one another;
even if one has mastered the Tripitaka through study or attained the realization of the four dhyānas through meditation.
One should contemplate non-arising and clarify the mind in the principle of emptiness;
if one does not protect one's life, [how can one attain this?]
Even if you uphold the teachings according to the instructions,
in the end you will not escape the Buddha’s reproach for the first of the ten evil offenses.
Who would take its place and receive it?
Furthermore, suppose one sees a butcher leading a sheep into a temple;
it will not take more than a few mouthfuls.
He released it, calling it "Long Life.
The assembly gathered together to watch;
they snapped their fingers and exclaimed, "Excellent!"
How can one know that the water used within the quarters kills thousands and tens of thousands of living beings every day?
Once this principle and teaching are known, one must not treat it lightly.
One should examine and investigate with great care;
benefiting oneself and others,
one should guard well and reflect well.
Furthermore, there are those who cause people to plow fields and plant crops,
seeking only small profits while failing to see the great transgression involved.
Both creatures of water and land were harmed;
countless beings were killed.
Such is the gravity of this transgression.
What can be done? It is as if one were already bound hand and foot at the gates of the underworld,
leaving one's fate entirely to his disposal.
Therefore, a sutra states:
"A person who takes life shall fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals."
Even if one should obtain human birth,
one will have a short lifespan and many ailments.
Alas, what suffering this is!
Who shall receive it?
If there be one capable of doing so,
excellent, most excellent!
This may be called the Final Dharma age of Śākyamuni;
together we have bound the cause for compassionate mindfulness,
so that when Maitreya first attains enlightenment, [we shall be reborn].
Both realized the fruit of non-arising;
as this is explained extensively in other biographies,
there is no need for further elaboration here.
The Ritual Procedures for Protecting Life and Releasing Captured Creatures (Mṛtyupālanamokṣaṇavidhi)
